archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (goaltending-sunk)
archetype.definition: A team that out-shoots and out-chances nearly everyone at 5-on-5 and runs an elite power play, but its goaltending and penalty kill are giving back the edge, leaving it at a .500-ish record its underlying play doesn't deserve.

report.headline: Elite process, bottom-tier saves: Utah's slide is a goaltending problem
report.take:
Utah is one of the best puck-possession teams in the league right now, and its record doesn't show it. The Mammoth own a 0.568 xGF % (2nd) and a 0.54 CF % (4th). They put 29.3 shots a game on net (6th) and allow only 24.7 (5th). The power play converts at 34.7%, second in the league. Teams that tilt the ice this way usually sit near the top of the standings. Instead Utah is 10-8-3, fifth in a crowded Central, tied with Winnipeg and 15th on the site.

The gap is in net. Team Goalies GSAx is -11.7, 31st of 32, and the all-situations save % is .869, 30th. Neither goalie is clear of it: Karel Vejmelka is at .872 and -6.8 GSAx over 14 starts, Sebastian Cossa at .863 and -5.2 over 7. The goaltending grade is a D-, against a B+ forward group and an A blueline led by Mikhail Sergachev, 7th on the defensemen tab with 22 points. A 70.4% penalty kill (27th) makes it worse, because the few chances Utah does allow are turning into goals at a high rate. The result is 3.57 goals allowed a game, 27th, behind a shot-suppression profile that should produce something far better.

The numbers mostly point one way: this is bad luck as much as bad play. The 5-on-5 PDO is 97.5, and the shooting side is ordinary, with skaters at .115 against a .114 league mark. That means the drag is almost all save percentage. Pts vs Goal Diff is a neutral 0.8, so the record isn't propped up or held down by close-game luck; the goal differential itself is the problem. Last season the same franchise had +14.1 GSAx and the 10th-ranked defense. A swing that large in net tends to come partway back. The one offensive number to be wary of is Logan Cooley's 11 goals on 31 shots, which will cool. Nick Schmaltz (-14, 0.452 xGF %) and Dylan Guenther (-12) are also bleeding goals in their minutes, while the Hayton and Lee depth minutes (0.641 and 0.622 xGF %) are quietly dominant.

The last two weeks have been ugly: 0-2-3 over the last five, allowing 4.2 goals a game. Three of those losses came past regulation, including a 0-1 overtime loss to St. Louis and a 5-6 overtime loss to San Jose. That is a team losing coin flips because its goalie isn't stealing any. If even league-average goaltending shows up, the possession numbers suggest a team that climbs back into a top-three Central spot. If it doesn't, Utah can tread water around the 90-point pace it is on now.

strengths.title: Owns the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Utah ranks near the top in both shot-attempt share and expected-goal share. It also suppresses shots better than all but a handful of teams. That points to structure and depth: the Hayton and Lee minutes and the whole blueline post strong xGF % numbers, so this isn't one line carrying the load. Process numbers like these are the most durable thing a team has.

strengths.title: A lethal power play
strengths.body: The power play converts at 34.7%, well above the 22.2% league average. Clayton Keller has 16 PP points and Sergachev, Cooley and Schmaltz each have 12. Some regression from a rate that high is inevitable, but the volume of talent on the top unit means it should stay a top-five weapon.

strengths.title: An A-grade blueline
strengths.body: Sergachev plays 24.53 minutes a night and ranks 7th among defensemen with 22 points. Weegar, Schmidt and Marino all post xGF % numbers near or above 0.59. This group is the engine of the shot suppression and should stay that way.

concerns.title: Goaltending is near the league floor
concerns.body: Both goalies are well below expected. Vejmelka sits at -6.8 GSAx and Cossa at -5.2, for a team save % of .869 that ranks 30th. That is the single biggest reason a team allowing so few shots ranks 27th in goals allowed a game. Last season's +14.1 GSAx suggests this should improve, but neither goalie has yet earned the net.

concerns.title: Penalty kill leaks
concerns.body: A 70.4% kill ranks 27th, well under the 77.4% league average and a step down from 78.1% last season. Some of that is the same goaltending problem showing up shorthanded. Still, it gives back much of what the power play earns.

concerns.title: Slide has cost real ground
concerns.body: After a 9-5 October, Utah went 0-2-3 over its last five, getting outscored and allowing 4.2 goals a game. Possession hasn't collapsed, but points lost in a division this tight are hard to recover. A few top-six forwards, notably Schmaltz at -14, are on the wrong end of their minutes.

trend.note: A strong October gave way to a winless five-game run in mid-November. The goaltending kept leaking while the shot metrics held up, so the drop is in results more than in play.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, starting with the league's worst team
weekAhead.body:
The schedule is a chance to stop the bleeding. Vancouver comes in last on the site at 4-17-1. The Canucks rank last in xGF %, last in PK % at 62%, and last in Goalies GSAx, so Utah's power play and shot volume should feast there. Anaheim is the other soft spot in net, with an F goaltending grade and a .865 save %, though its league-best power play is a real threat to Utah's weak kill.

Colorado is the stiff test. The Avalanche have A+ forwards and the second-ranked offense, and they will punish any goaltending lapse. The week closes in Winnipeg against a team with the identical 10-8-3 record. The Jets give up 32 shots a game, the most in the league, and that plays straight into Utah's strength. Anything less than five or six points from this stretch would be a disappointment given the matchups.

keyMatchups.title: Utah power play vs. Vancouver's kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts at 34.7%, and Vancouver kills just 62%, worst in the league. The Canucks also allow the most points to forwards relative to expectation. This is the game to reset the scoreboard.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's kill vs. Anaheim's power play
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim's power play leads the league at 35.2%, and Utah's 70.4% kill ranks 27th. Special teams could decide the game by themselves. Staying out of the box matters more here than anywhere else this week.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume in Winnipeg
keyMatchups.body: Winnipeg allows 32 shots a game, last in the league, and its goaltending is only a C. Utah's possession game should generate plenty in a head-to-head with a division rival on the same record.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Vejmelka or Cossa strings together league-average save percentages. The rest of the team is already doing enough to win.

restOfSeason.body:
The possession and shot-suppression numbers are the most reliable signals on the sheet, and they describe a top-tier team. The .869 team save % is very unlikely to persist over 61 more games: the league average is .892 and this franchise was well above expected in net last season. Even partial recovery should pull goals against back toward the middle of the league. Expect the power play to come down from 34.7% and Cooley's finishing to cool, which trims some offense.

Net of those moves, Utah should play like a solid playoff team the rest of the way. The hole it has dug, and a Central with Minnesota, Dallas and Colorado ahead of it, keeps the final number from being spectacular. The range depends almost entirely on the crease: middling goaltending lands roughly 92-95 points, while continued bottom-three goaltending caps it near the current 90-point pace.
swingFactors: Whether either goalie reaches league-average save %
Penalty-kill recovery toward last season's level
Top-six forwards like Schmaltz and Guenther winning their minutes

confidence.note: 21 games is small for save %, but the possession edge is large and consistent.
